strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically important problem: attributing concept shift (changes in p(y|X)) to a sparse set of features in tabular data, complementing prior work on covariate/label shift and on shift detection without attribution

Method is well-motivated and modular: the GAM offset formulation keeps the source model intact (works with black-box base models), and the three extensions (absorption term for misspecification, knockoffs for FDR control, and their combination) are sensible and clearly presented

Provides statistical guarantees: a convergence bound for the ℓ1-penalized shift estimator (Theorem 4.1) and FDR/PFER control for the derandomized knockoff procedure (Lemma 4.2), with proofs in the appendix

Extensive semi-synthetic evaluation across three real healthcare datasets with realistic feature correlations, 16 generator/base model combinations, multiple sample sizes, and 100 replicates; results show consistent and substantial gains over constructed baselines (Diff, WhyShift, SHAP-adapted)

Real-data analysis is more than a toy demonstration: the sparsity claim is empirically validated via loss-recovery curves (Figure 2/7), and the COVID-19 Omicron case study recovers feature shifts consistent with the medical literature
Reproducibility is well supported: code, preprocessing pipelines, hyperparameters, and data access instructions are provided, including for the restricted All of Us data
weaknesses: The semi-synthetic evaluation favors the method by construction: induced shifts are additive perturbations of g(E[y|X]) on selected features, which is exactly the shift model SGShift assumes. There is no evaluation under shift types that violate the additive-GAM assumption (e.g., interaction-based or non-additive shifts), so the claimed robustness 'when this assumption falters' is only weakly supported

Ground-truth evaluation relies almost entirely on semi-synthetic relabeling; the only real-data assessment (Figure 3) is qualitative and without ground truth, and there is no empirical validation that the discovered features actually drive the measured performance drop

Theoretical results are standard adaptations of classical lasso/stability-selection analysis, with some gaps: (i) the sub-Gaussian i.i.d. assumption on ϕi conflicts with the fact that ϕ(X) are deterministic basis functions of real (correlated, non-Gaussian) tabular features; (ii) the FDR proof invokes independence of selection events across knockoff realizations and a 'geometric thinning inequality' from [RWC23] whose applicability to this setting is not carefully established; (iii) the FDR derivation is loose (bounding FDR of the thresholded set by the sum of V[b])

Baselines are weak or self-constructed: Diff is introduced by the authors, and the SHAP adaptation is crude; more relevant competitors such as SJS [CZZ22] or the causal-parent-set approach of [ZSGJ23] are discussed in related work but not empirically compared

Knockoff construction quality on real, correlated tabular data is a known difficulty for Model-X knockoffs and directly affects the validity of the FDR guarantee, yet this practical issue is not analyzed or discussed; likewise, sensitivity to λ/π hyperparameter choices is not studied

Baseline SGShift (without knockoffs) has quite low recall (~0.4-0.5) at FPR 10%; the headline results depend heavily on the knockoff variants, and Table 2 reports no variance, making the magnitude of some differences (e.g., SGShift-K vs. SGShift-KA) hard to judge

Some overstatement relative to the literature (e.g., 'No existing method aims to attribute exactly what features contribute to this shift' overlooks [ZSGJ23]), and minor presentation issues (typos such as 'koint distribution', inconsistent conditions in Theorem 4.1)

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and underexplored problem: attributing concept shift (changes in p(y|X)) to a sparse set of features, which is practically useful for diagnosing model failure in deployment settings such as healthcare.

The method is sensible and modular: a sparse GAM correction term on top of an arbitrary source model, with well-motivated extensions (an absorption term for model misspecification, and derandomized knockoffs for false discovery control).

The empirical evaluation is broad in scope: three real-world healthcare datasets with natural domain splits, 16 generator/base model configurations, sample-size ablations, and 100 replicates with confidence intervals, and supplementary material includes detailed per-configuration results and hyperparameters.
The real-data case study on the Delta-to-Omicron shift (Figure 3) grounds the method's output in external medical literature, providing qualitative face validity for the selected features.
Code and preprocessing pipelines are reportedly provided in the supplementary material, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is largely an adaptation of standard lasso/RSC analysis, and its assumptions are strained: the theory requires the basis functions ϕ_i to be i.i.d. sub-Gaussian with covariance Σ ≻ 0, which is unrealistic for basis expansions of real covariates (which are fixed, correlated, and often deterministic transformations), and the sample-complexity requirement n_T ≳ a log K is not discussed relative to the small target domains actually used.

The treatment of the offset model ˆf is too casual. Remark 4 asserts the offset does not affect RSC, but the approximation error of the working model ˆf relative to the true f enters the gradient/subgradient bound (∥∇L(δ*)∥∞ ≤ c3λ) and the effective noise level; the proof does not trace this dependency, so the convergence guarantee as stated does not clearly cover the misspecified-model case that motivates SGShift-A.

The proof of Lemma 4.2 (FDR control) is questionable. The step 'since Π̂_k ≥ π ⟹ Σ_b 1{k ∈ Â^[b]} ≥ Bπ' yields only a lower bound on Σ_b V^[b], yet it is used as an upper bound in FDR(Aˆ(π)) ≤ E[Σ_b V^[b] / Bπ]. The claim that 'each feature's selection events are independent across B iterations' is also false in general: knockoff realizations are independent conditional on X, but selections share the same finite-sample data noise and are therefore positively correlated. The reliance on a 'geometric thinning inequality' from [RWC23] needs to be verified as applicable to this setting, not merely cited.

The semi-synthetic evaluation is favorably matched to the method's inductive bias by construction: the ground-truth shift is induced exactly as an additive perturbation of g(E[y|X]) through additive transformations of selected features, which is precisely the model class SGShift fits. No experiments probe performance under non-additive shifts, interactions, or distributional changes of a different structural form, so the claim that 'true concept shifts tend to be sparse' is partially circular.

Baselines are weak and partially self-constructed. The 'Diff' baseline is built by the authors, WhyShift and SHAP are adapted rather than used as published, and the directly-related SJS framework [CZZ22] is discussed in related work but not compared empirically. There is also a conceptual tension: the SHAP-based explanation-shift detector [MBM+23] is described as not using target outcomes, yet the adapted 'SHAP' baseline is trained on both domains.

The abstract's headline claim ('AUC > 0.9 and recall > 90%, often 2 or 3 times as high as baseline methods') overstates the typical results: recall above 90% is achieved only by the knockoff variants under matched settings on some datasets, while plain SGShift recall is often 0.4–0.5 (Tables 4–9), and the wide confidence intervals in Figure 1 substantially qualify the aggregate gains.

The real-data 'validation' (Figures 2–3) lacks ground truth, and the sparsity evidence is indirect: an elbow in log-loss recovery as features are added does not uniquely establish that the underlying shift is sparse in features rather than in some other representation. Interpretations of specific features (e.g., respiratory failure) are plausible but post-hoc.

Presentation has enough errors to impede careful reading: typos ('Regardless the amount', 'an an underlying', 'koint distribution'), a seemingly mismatched citation for GAMs ([Has17] pointing to 'Statistical models in S'), an inconsistent reference [MDSR25] (NeurIPS volume 37 dated 2025), and Theorem 4.1's constants (C depending on c1, c2, c3) hiding the dependence on the sub-Gaussian norm and κ that determines actual sample requirements.

The limitations discussion is thin: the sparsity assumption's failure modes, sensitivity to the choice of basis functions ϕ_j, λ tuning in practice (how λ_ω < λ_δ is selected without ground truth), and the absence of comparison to [CZZ22] are acknowledged only briefly or not at all.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely useful and underexplored problem: attributing concept shift (changes in p(y|X)) to a sparse set of features, complementing the large literature on detecting/correcting covariate shift. The framing of the shift as a sparse GAM update on top of a fixed source model is simple, interpretable, and works even with black-box base models.

The method family is well-motivated and layered: the absorption term (SGShift-A) to absorb model misspecification via a difference-in-difference structure and the knockoff-based variant (SGShift-K/KA) with derandomization via stability selection are sensible extensions, with hierarchical regularization (λ_ω < λ_δ) thoughtfully prioritizing concept shift over model misfit.

The empirical study is comprehensive: three real healthcare datasets with natural domain splits (temporal, population, outcome), 16 generator/base model combinations per dataset, matched and misspecified settings, sample-size ablations, and 100 replicates. SGShift variants consistently and substantially outperform the baselines (Diff, WhyShift, SHAP) across configurations.
The semi-synthetic simulation design is careful in preserving real feature correlations and keeping P_S(X) = P_T(X) so the induced shift is purely conditional, isolating concept shift.

The real-world COVID-19 analysis (Figure 3) recovers feature-level findings consistent with published medical literature on Omicron vs. Delta severity, and Figure 2 provides evidence that natural concept shifts in these datasets are indeed sparse, empirically supporting the core sparsity hypothesis.

Code, preprocessing pipelines, hyperparameters, and data-fetching scripts are provided, supporting reproducibility; the restricted-access COVID data is handled appropriately with documented access procedures.
The paper honestly acknowledges limitations, including that dense concept shifts may exist and be difficult to explain under the sparsity assumption.
weaknesses: The theoretical contributions are largely straightforward adaptations of standard results. Theorem 4.1 is a conventional lasso estimation error bound under RSC applied to the offset setting, and the PFER part of Lemma 4.2 is direct stability selection analysis. The novelty of the theory relative to [LCL22, LCD23], [MB10], and [RWC23] is incremental.

The theory's assumptions do not match the method's practical use. The RSC proof (A.1) assumes the basis vectors ϕ_i are i.i.d. sub-Gaussian with Σ ≻ 0 and requires ∇²_η ℓ ≥ κ > 0 uniformly — the latter is false for logistic loss (the Hessian vanishes for extreme η), so the claimed curvature condition needs a restricted or bounded-η argument that is not given. In practice ϕ are deterministic transformations of real, non-sub-Gaussian features, so the guarantee does not directly cover the experimental setting.

The theory provides only estimation-error control, not support recovery or selection consistency, yet the paper's central claims are about identifying the shifted feature set A. There is no guarantee linking δ̂'s support to the true support, which is the actual inferential target.

The FDR control proof of Lemma 4.2 has a gap: it relies on the geometric thinning inequality justified by 'independence of each feature's selection events across B iterations,' but knockoff realizations share the same data (X, y), so selection events across b are correlated through the shared statistics; the required independence is asserted rather than established. The exchangeability argument also needs care when knockoffs are applied to the basis functions ϕ(X) rather than raw X.

The semi-synthetic evaluation may favor the proposed method: induced shifts are constructed as additive perturbations of g(E[y|X]) on selected features, closely matching SGShift's additive sparse-update model class, while the baselines (particularly Diff, a baseline constructed by the authors) are comparatively weak and less matched to the ground truth. This biases the '2-3x recall' claims, and the claim that no existing method attributes features to concept shift is overstated given WhyShift and SJS output feature-level information.

The theory does not account for the error in the working model f̂ converging to f; the offset is treated as exact in the analysis, whereas misspecification of f̂ is precisely one of the failure modes the absorption term is designed to address, and its interaction with the guarantees is unanalyzed.

Real-data evaluation is qualitative only (feature rankings in Figure 3) with no ground truth, and the real-data sparsity evidence (Figure 2, elbow-shaped recovery) is shown for only a subset of models with results deferred to the appendix.

Recall is evaluated only at a fixed FPR of 10%, and aggregate results mask configuration-level variance; the abstract's headline claims (AUC > 0.9, recall > 90%) apply mainly to the knockoff variants in favorable configurations.

Presentation issues: minor but noticeable typos ('koint distribution', 'Regardless the amount'), inconsistent lemma numbering ('Lemma .1'), and the absorption term's design choices (basis functions, the λ_ω < λ_δ ordering) are heuristic and not systematically ablated.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and under-served problem—attributing performance degradation under concept shift to specific features—directly, rather than as a secondary use of other tools. The framing of concept shift as learning a sparse correction to a fixed source model is clean and enables reuse of mature statistical machinery (GAMs, lasso, Model-X knockoffs, e-BH derandomization).

Three method variants are well-motivated: SGShift (Bearer [REDACTED] correction), SGShift-A (absorbing shared source-model misspecification via a hierarchical penalty), and SGShift-K (knockoff-based selection with false discovery control). The decomposition of misspecification vs. target-specific shift is a sensible modeling idea.

The evaluation is unusually extensive: 48 semi-synthetic settings spanning multiple base/generator model pairs and three real datasets, plus stress tests for high dimension, feature correlation, SNR, dense shifts violating the sparsity assumption, global calibration shifts, and interaction shifts. SGShift variants consistently and substantially outperform the baselines.

The real-data case studies (COVID-19 pre/post-Omicron, Lupus across ancestries, ACS cross-state splits) recover shifts consistent with the medical/genetics literature, and the IPW experiments usefully rule out covariate/label shift as the primary explanation of the observed degradation.

The paper is appropriately honest about the scope of its theory: it claims estimation consistency only, explicitly disclaims support recovery for Bearer [REDACTED], and labels the Appendix F penalty calibration as a heuristic.

Reproducibility is reasonably addressed: dataset splits, sample sizes, hyperparameters, and preprocessing are documented, and code/data availability is stated (with appropriate handling of the restricted-access All of Us data).
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees are largely standard lasso-style results, and the assumptions do not clearly cover the paper's main use case. Lemma A.1 assumes the loss has curvature bounded below by κ > 0, which fails for logistic loss (whose second derivative vanishes in the tails)—yet binary classification is a primary task. Moreover, Theorem 3.1 requires λ ≥ 2‖∇L(δ*)‖∞, while the practical default selects λ by cross-validation, so the theory and the deployed procedure are not aligned.

The FDR guarantee in Theorem 3.3 has notable gaps: the per-repeat false-selection probability bound α is assumed rather than derived, and independence of selection events across knockoff repeats conditional on the data is assumed. It is also unclear whether the knockoff sign-flip/exchangeability property is preserved given that λ is tuned on target labels, which would break the Y-independence needed for the formal guarantee.

Identifiability for SGShift-A is not established. With both a shared correction ω and target-specific δ fit simultaneously, the split between 'source misspecification' and 'true concept shift' is only enforced through an ad hoc hierarchy (λω = cλδ, c < 1); Theorem 3.2 characterizes a population minimizer without arguing that δ* corresponds to the actual shift when the model class is misspecified, which is the stated motivation for SGShift-A.

Baselines are comparatively weak: Diff is constructed by the authors, and closely related published methods discussed in the related work (Singh et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2023) are not empirically compared against, making the 'greatly superior performance' claim harder to calibrate.

Real-data claims rest on plausibility rather than ground truth. The COVID-19 and Lupus findings are consistent with prior literature, but the attribution of individual selected features (e.g., 'insurance claims', 'age 45–64') is post-hoc interpretation; there is no validation that the selected feature sets are correct in these settings.

Some experimental aggregation practices reduce interpretability: Table 1 averages AUC across heterogeneous model configurations with CIs across (not within) configurations, and dense-shift results for SGShift-K (AUC > 0.9 despite >60% of features shifted) are explained informally as a ranking effect, in which case the FDR guarantee does not apply in that regime.

Writing contains minor errors and informal passages (e.g., 'generator model"', 'koint distribution', typos), and the discussion of why the ε-BH aggregated procedure's assumptions hold for these knockoff statistics is deferred thinly to Appendix E.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely important and under-explored problem: attributing concept shift (changes in P(Y|X)) to specific features without requiring prespecified causal graphs. The framing as sparse correction to a fixed source model is clean and practical.

The experimental scope is broad: 3 real healthcare datasets, 48 semi-synthetic settings varying base/generator models, plus dedicated stress tests for high dimensionality, feature correlation, SNR, global calibration shifts, and interaction shifts.

Theory coverage is more complete than many applied papers: estimation consistency (Thm 3.1), an analogous result for SGShift-A (Thm 3.2), and false discovery control via stability selection and derandomized knockoffs (Thm 3.3), with honest disclaimers that exact support recovery is not claimed.

The real-data analyses (COVID-19 pre/post-Omicron, Lupus ancestry study, ACS income) are engaging, and the authors usefully check whether covariate/label shift alone (via IPW) can explain performance drops before attributing to concept shift.

Reproducibility is reasonably treated: hyperparameters, seeds, dataset splits, and preprocessing are documented, and code/preprocessed data are stated to be released (with appropriate handling of restricted-access All of Us data).
weaknesses: Evaluation circularity: the semi-synthetic shifts are constructed by perturbing g(E[Y|X]) as an additive correction on the link scale — exactly the model class SGShift assumes (Eq. 1). The benchmark therefore structurally favors the proposed method over baselines like WhyShift or SHAP, so the claimed 'greatly superior performance' does not establish robustness to realistic, non-additive concept shifts. This is the paper's central evidential weakness.

The methodological novelty is limited: SGShift is essentially a Lasso on target-domain data with the source model's predictions as a fixed offset — a minor variation on standard sparse regression — and Theorem 3.1's proof (Appendix B) is a textbook Lasso argument. The offset observation does not require new theory since h_S(X) is just a known function of X.

Theorem 3.2 raises identifiability concerns: the target-domain augmented rows are z_T = (φ(X_T), φ(X_T)), so the two blocks are perfectly collinear in the target loss, which depends only on ω+δ. Local RSC/RE conditions on such a rank-deficient augmented design appear suspect; identification rests entirely on source rows, yet Appendix C offers only a proof sketch and never verifies the cone condition is satisfiable.

The FDR control is not fully convincing: Theorem 3.3's PFER bound assumes per-repeat selection probability α ≤ threshold and independence across knockoff repeats conditional on the data (assumptions acknowledged but not verified), and the empirical table in Appendix E shows FDR exceeding nominal levels (0.10, 0.15 in dense settings) with power collapsing for Diabetes (0.21–0.42). Model-X knockoff validity on correlated real healthcare features (e.g., second-order knockoffs) is also not validated.

The real-data 'concept shift' conclusions are interpretive rather than verified: there is no ground truth, and the SUPPORT2 split (survivors vs. in-hospital deaths) changes the label distribution by construction, conflating label shift with concept shift despite the IPW correction check. In the Lupus case, the European model reports AUC 1.0, suggesting overfitting/leakage with 149 samples and 1000 genes, which undermines the reliability of the discovered 'shifted genes.'

Baselines are comparatively weak or repurposed: 'Diff' is constructed by the authors themselves, SHAP is adapted beyond its design, and WhyShift is used for feature-level ranking when it was proposed to locate regions of covariate space. A comparison against stronger conditional-shift attribution methods (e.g., Singh et al. 2024/2025) is missing.

The λ-selection story is informal: CV when prediction is the goal, a ranking across λ or a heuristic (Appendix F) when selection is the goal; Appendix F's one-pass mFDR rule relies on orthogonal-design and homoskedastic approximations that are acknowledged but whose practical accuracy is not evaluated.

There is no dedicated limitations section; caveats are scattered (e.g., knockoff validity with interaction bases, non-identifiability of causal mechanisms, heuristic calibration), which understates the conditions under which the central claims hold.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly posed problem: attributing concept shift (changes in p(Y|X)) to a sparse set of features is a practically important and underexplored diagnosis task, and the paper positions itself carefully against existing covariate-shift and explanation-shift work.

The core reframing — learning a sparse target-domain correction on top of a fixed source model, rather than a noisy difference-of-two-plugin-models — is a clean, sensible idea that directly addresses the error-accumulation problem of plugin approaches like WhyShift, and is supported empirically (Table 1 shows consistent AUC gains across 48 settings).

Three complementary variants are developed: plain SGShift, SGShift-A with an absorption term to mitigate source-model misspecification, and SGShift-K with Model-X knockoffs and derandomized e-BH aggregation for FDR control. This gives practitioners options with different guarantees.

The evaluation is unusually thorough: sparse and dense shifts, model match/mismatch, varying target sample sizes, high-dimensional and correlated-feature regimes, SNR sweeps, global calibration shifts, and interaction shifts (Appendices J and K), plus explicit checks that covariate/label shift (via IPW) cannot explain the observed performance drops on real data.

Real-data case studies (COVID-19 pre/post-Omicron, Lupus across ancestries, 87 ACS income cross-state cases) recover findings consistent with the medical/genetics literature, and the paper is appropriately careful that SGShift identifies predictive differences rather than causal mechanisms.

Reproducibility is treated seriously: preprocessing code is released, the restricted-access data handling is documented, hyperparameters are listed (Appendix H), and sensitivity to λ and the λω/λδ ratio is reported.
weaknesses: The theoretical results are essentially standard Lasso/M-estimation analysis transplanted to the correction term. Theorem 3.1 requires the well-specified model in Equation 1 (exact linear basis representation of the shift), and Theorem 3.2 is only a proof sketch with the augmented-design RSC assumed rather than established. The Appendix A RSC justification glosses over the local curvature condition (Hessian lower bound is stated on a neighborhood rather than derived from the loss).

Theorem 3.3's PFER control relies on a per-repeat false-selection probability bound α that is assumed, never verified or estimated, and the conditional independence of repeated knockoff selections given the data is asserted rather than justified. Moreover, the reported empirical FDR in Appendix E reaches 0.15 (dense, mismatched SUPPORT2), which exceeds a typical nominal level, suggesting the guarantee may not hold tightly in the regimes practitioners care about.

The semi-synthetic evaluation induces shifts by additively perturbing g(E[Y|X]) — exactly the additive, link-scale correction model class that SGShift assumes. This plausibly favors SGShift over baselines (e.g., tree-based WhyShift) in a way that may not generalize to non-additive or structural shifts; only one shift-generation mechanism is tested on the real datasets.

The baseline set is relatively weak and largely repurposed (Diff, SHAP, WhyShift); no comparison against the more directly related hierarchical decomposition methods (Singh et al., 2024/2025) or causal-parent-set approaches (Zhang et al., 2023), which are cited as closely related.

There is some conflation between 'attribution' and 'correction' in the real-data analysis: the sparse-update finding (90% of performance loss recovered with few features) shows a sparse correction exists, not that the identified features are the truly shifted ones; identifiability of the true shift support from unpaired source/target data is not formally addressed beyond the well-specified case.

SGShift-K's strong performance comes at the cost of losing simultaneous model correction (the paper itself notes this), and its power degrades noticeably at low SNR; the trade-off between variants is discussed only briefly.

Presentation issues: some key implementation details (λ selection heuristic, grouping of nonlinear basis functions for knockoffs) are deferred to appendices that read as heuristic and somewhat informal relative to the main-text guarantee claims.
